title: Concept Drills — Basic Concept of Organic Chemistry (Class 11 Chemistry)
subject: chemistry

questions.concept: Why carbon is organic chemistry's backbone
questions.question: What three properties of carbon make it uniquely suited to build millions of compounds?
questions.solution: (1) TETRAVALENCY — four bonds, allowing branched and cyclic frameworks. (2) CATENATION — strong C–C bonds let chains and rings grow long. (3) MULTIPLE BONDING — stable single, double and triple bonds, plus bonding to H, O, N, S, halogens. No other element combines all three.

questions.question: Why does adding one CH₂ to a homologous series change physical properties steadily but chemical properties barely at all?
questions.solution: Each CH₂ adds mass and surface (van der Waals forces rise → boiling point climbs steadily) but the FUNCTIONAL GROUP — the reactive site — is unchanged. Chemistry lives in the functional group; physics lives in the whole molecule. That is why a series shares reactions but not boiling points.

questions.question: Name CH₃–CH(CH₃)–CH₂–CH₃ by IUPAC rules and state the three decisions the name encodes.
questions.solution: Longest chain = 4 carbons → butane. Numbering from the end nearer the branch gives the methyl the lowest locant: 2-methylbutane (not 3-methylbutane). The name encodes: (1) chain length (parent), (2) substituent identity and position (locant), (3) the numbering rule — lowest set of locants wins. Systematic naming is a compressed structural description.

questions.question: C₄H₁₀ has two isomers. What makes them different compounds, and why do their boiling points differ?
questions.solution: Same molecular formula but different ATOM CONNECTIVITY: n-butane (straight chain) vs isobutane (branched). The branched isomer is more compact — less surface contact, weaker van der Waals forces — so it boils ~11 °C lower. Connectivity changes shape; shape changes intermolecular forces.

questions.concept: Fission of bonds — homolytic vs heterolytic
questions.question: A C–X bond can break two ways. Name both, the species each produces, and which solvents favour which.
questions.solution: Homolytic fission: each fragment takes one electron → free radicals (favoured by non-polar solvents, UV light, high temperature). Heterolytic fission: one fragment takes both → cation + anion (favoured by polar solvents that stabilise ions). The breaking mode determines whether the reaction follows a radical or ionic mechanism.

questions.question: Carbon forms millions of compounds while silicon, below it in the group, forms far fewer. Give the two key reasons.
questions.solution: (1) C–C bonds are strong and stable, allowing long chains and rings; Si–Si bonds are much weaker and cleave readily. (2) Carbon is small enough to form stable multiple bonds (C=C, C≡C) and to pack densely in many geometries. Versatility comes from the strength and smallness of carbon bonds — not from carbon being 'special', but from the numbers working out.

questions.question: Ethane and ethanol differ by one oxygen atom yet belong to different chemical families with entirely different properties. Why does a small group dominate behaviour?
questions.solution: Physical and chemical properties are controlled by the SITE of reactivity and by polarity. The –OH group introduces hydrogen bonding (higher boiling point, water solubility) and a nucleophilic oxygen (oxidation, esterification), so reactions occur there rather than on the hydrocarbon frame, which is comparatively inert. The hydrocarbon skeleton sets the shape and solubility trend; the functional group sets the chemistry. One group turns a nonpolar gas into a polar liquid.

questions.concept: Why homologous series show smooth trends
questions.question: Boiling points of alkanes rise smoothly with chain length. Why is the trend regular rather than erratic?
questions.solution: Each successive member adds one CH₂ unit, so the molecule's size, surface area and polarisability all increase in steps of the same amount. Van der Waals attraction grows with contact area, so boiling point rises steadily. Regularity comes from regular structural increments — a homologous series is a controlled experiment in chain length.
